tasks.q: Why is networking divided into layers?
a: To split a complex task into smaller, simpler tasks that work together
To make networks slower but safer
So only one protocol is ever used
tasks.fb: Each layer can focus on one job.

tasks.q: What does each layer do for the layer above it?
a: Encrypts it with a private key
tasks.fb: Each layer relies on the one below to do its job.

tasks.q: You change from Wi-Fi to an Ethernet cable. What else has to change?
a: Nothing else: only the bottom layer changes
tasks.fb: That's the point of layers: one can be swapped without affecting the others.

tasks.q: In the burger analogy, what does swapping beef for chicken show?
a: One layer can change without changing the others
All layers must be the same
tasks.fb: Just like protocols in different layers.

tasks.q: Which are advantages of layering protocols? Select all that apply.
opts: A layer can be changed without affecting the others
Problems can be traced to one layer
Different companies can make parts that work together
Networks no longer need any protocols
correct: A layer can be changed without affecting the others
Problems can be traced to one layer
Different companies can make parts that work together
tasks.fb: Layers still need protocols, and data can still go missing: TCP deals with that.

tasks.q: A network technician is troubleshooting. Why do layers help?
a: They can test one layer at a time to find where the problem is
They can remove all the layers
tasks.fb: Technicians often start at the bottom: is the cable plugged in?

tasks.q: Put the four layers in order, from top (closest to the user) to bottom.
tasks.fb: You don't need to name the layers for the J277 exam, but it helps to understand layering.

tasks.q: Which layer sends data over the actual cable or radio signal?
tasks.fb: The link layer covers Ethernet, Wi-Fi and the hardware.

tasks.q: Match each layer to the protocol used when sending an email over Wi-Fi.
tasks.fb: This is the second jigsaw from your workbook task.

tasks.q: Which protocol would be in the application layer when loading a web page?
tasks.fb: HTTP is used by the browser, which is an application.

tasks.q: Which layer would change if you moved from a school PC on a cable to a laptop on Wi-Fi?
Which layer does each protocol or technology belong to?
tasks.fb: Now RAG the revision checklist on your worksheet, ready for the end-of-unit assessment.

info.title: Seven or four?
info.text: There are two famous layer models: the 7-layer OSI model, used for teaching and troubleshooting, and the 4-layer TCP/IP model, which the internet actually uses.

info.title: Swap without breaking
info.text: When Wi-Fi 6 arrived, you didn't need new websites or browsers. Only the link layer changed, thanks to layering.

info.title: Start at the bottom
info.text: IT technicians often troubleshoot from the bottom layer up: is the cable plugged in? Is Wi-Fi connected? Only then do they check the apps.

info.title: Envelopes in envelopes
info.text: Each layer wraps the data with its own header, a bit like putting a letter in an envelope, then in a parcel. This is called encapsulation.

info.title: New protocols, same layers
info.text: The newest version of HTTP, HTTP/3, runs over a different transport protocol called QUIC, but the layers above and below didn't need to change.

info.title: Standards for each layer
info.text: Different organisations look after different layers, such as the IEEE for Ethernet and Wi-Fi, and the IETF for TCP/IP.
